blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints this heading as 1.4, but 1.4 is already the number of "Three Cube Roots of Unity" (book page 12). The next headings are also out of sequence (1.4.1, 1.3.3 and 1.5 are repeated numbers). We keep the printed numbers so you can find each part in your textbook; only the numbering is wrong, not the mathematics.

Up to now we have located points with Cartesian (rectangular) coordinates: an ordered pair \((x, y)\) tells us how far to go along the \(x\)-axis and then how far up or down. Polar coordinates describe the same point in a different way: how far is it from a fixed point, and in which direction?
Polar coordinates are often more convenient than Cartesian coordinates when a situation has circular or rotational symmetry, or when a problem depends on the distance from a fixed point and an angle measured from a reference direction.

blocks.alt: Polar grid: concentric circles of radius 1 to 4 around the pole O, the polar axis to the right marked 0 degrees, rays labelled pi/4 (45 degrees), pi/2 (90 degrees), 3pi/4 (135 degrees), pi (180 degrees), 5pi/4 (225 degrees), 3pi/2 (270 degrees) and 7pi/4 (315 degrees), and a point P(r, theta) on the pi/4 ray at distance r from O.
blocks.caption: Figure: the polar grid, with the pole O, the polar axis and a point P(r, θ) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text:
In the polar coordinate system the position of a point is fixed by two numbers:
1. a directed distance \(r\) from a fixed origin \(O\), called the pole, and
2. an angle \(\theta\) that the line joining the pole to the point makes with the polar axis (a fixed ray from the pole, usually taken along the positive \(x\)-axis).
In the polar coordinate system the location of a point \(P\) can be described by polar coordinates in the form \((r, \theta)\), where \(r\) and \(\theta\) are real numbers.

blocks.alt: Left: rectangular coordinates, point P(x, y) reached by going x along the x-axis and y up. Right: polar coordinates, the same kind of point P(r, theta) reached by a segment of length r from O making angle theta with the polar axis.
blocks.caption: Figure: a point in rectangular coordinates (x, y) and in polar coordinates (r, θ) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Think of a lighthouse beam or the hand of a clock fixed at the centre. To tell a friend where a ship is, you can say "5 km away, in the direction 45° from east". That is exactly a polar coordinate: \(r = 5\), \(\theta = 45^{\circ}\).
The angle is measured counter-clockwise from the polar axis. In this unit angles are usually written in radians: \(\pi\) radians \(= 180^{\circ}\).

blocks.caption: Teaching table (ours): common angles in degrees and radians

blocks.text:
Usually \(r\) is taken non-negative (\(r \ge 0\)), but \(r\) may also be negative (\(r < 0\)). The sign of \(r\) changes where the point lies in the plane.
When \(r > 0\): the angle \(\theta\) is the measure of any angle in standard position whose terminal side lies along the line from the origin to the point \(P\), measured counter-clockwise from the polar axis (positive \(x\)-axis).
For example, the polar coordinates \((5, \pi/4)\) represent a point 5 units away from the pole at an angle of \(\pi/4\) radians.

blocks.alt: The point P(5, pi/4): a segment of length 5 from the pole O at an angle of pi/4 above the polar axis.
blocks.caption: Figure: P(5, π/4) is 5 units from the pole at angle π/4 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text:
When \(r < 0\): the angle \(\theta\) is still the angle of the line through the origin, but the point \(Q\) is located \(|r|\) units in the opposite direction, that is, in the direction \(\theta + \pi\) from the polar axis.
For example, the polar coordinates \((-5, \pi/4)\) represent a point 5 units away from the pole, but in the direction of
\[\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \pi = \dfrac{5\pi}{4} \text{ radians.}\]

blocks.alt: The point Q(-5, pi/4): the ray at angle pi/4 is dashed; Q lies 5 units from O in the opposite direction, at angle pi/4 + pi = 5pi/4, in the third quadrant. An arc shows the turn of 5pi/4 from the polar axis.
blocks.caption: Figure: Q(−5, π/4) lies 5 units from the pole in the direction π/4 + π = 5π/4 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: \((-5, \pi/4)\) and \((5, 5\pi/4)\) represent the same point in the plane.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why are they the same point? Turn both into rectangular coordinates with \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\) (you will meet these in 1.4.1):
For \((-5, \pi/4)\):
\[x = -5\cos\tfrac{\pi}{4} = -\tfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[y = -5\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4} = -\tfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\]
For \((5, 5\pi/4)\):
\[x = 5\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{4} = -\tfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[y = 5\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{4} = -\tfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\]
Both give \(x = y = -\tfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \approx -3.54\): the same point in the third quadrant.
Also, a full turn \(2\pi\) brings you back to the same direction, so \((5, \pi/4)\), \((5, 9\pi/4)\) and \((5, -7\pi/4)\) are all the same point. A point has many polar names; that is why the next topic chooses one standard angle, the principal argument.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
• Polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\): distance \(r\) from the pole \(O\), angle \(\theta\) from the polar axis.
• The polar axis is usually the positive \(x\)-axis; angles are measured counter-clockwise.
• \(r > 0\): go \(r\) units in the direction \(\theta\).
• \(r < 0\): go \(|r|\) units in the opposite direction \(\theta + \pi\).
• \((-r, \theta)\) and \((r, \theta + \pi)\) name the same point; adding \(2\pi\) to \(\theta\) also gives the same point.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
• Measuring the angle clockwise. Positive angles go counter-clockwise from the polar axis.
• For \(r < 0\), plotting the point in the direction \(\theta\) itself. It goes the opposite way, in the direction \(\theta + \pi\).
• Mixing degrees and radians: \(\pi/4\) means \(45^{\circ}\), not 0.785 degrees.
• Thinking a point has only one pair \((r, \theta)\). It has infinitely many.
